title: Make a role's invocation match the grant it holds, and protect the args-derivation property in CI

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Audited 17461bb on main; working tree clean apart from .vscode/settings.json. Sprint file read fresh at audit time.

Reqs 1, 2, 3 and 5 are met, and Req 2 is met in the strong sense the criterion asks for. Req 4 is not, and I can show it: the defect that requirement exists to guard against can be present with your entire suite green.

================================================================
BLOCKER — REQ 4. THE CI TEST DOES NOT PROTECT THE PROPERTY IT NAMES.
scripts/launcher_test.js:2501 (the Sprint 31 Req 4 test)
================================================================

Req 4: "the emitted record is derived from the values actually passed to the child rather than reassembled from a second source — is protected by a test that runs in CI." The criterion closes: "A test that recomputes what it is checking would pass while the defect it guards against is present."

I introduced exactly that defect and ran the suite. One edit, in emitPermissionRecord, replacing the args-derived allowedTools with one rebuilt from HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES — the literal "second source" the requirement names:

    allowedTools: HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES[role.id].allowedTools.join(' ')

    node scripts/launcher_test.js  ->  ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED

Not just your Req 4 test. The whole suite. The record was reassembled from a second source and nothing in CI noticed.

WHY, and this is the part that matters: in this repo the profile-joined string and the args string are byte-identical for all six roles. No fullyCompletely.testCommand is declared and no ownedRepository grant is in force, so needsTestCommand and the owned-repository branch both append nothing. Two sources that produce the same bytes cannot be told apart by any comparison between them — including a comparison against the child's real argv, because the child received that same identical string. The test compares a value to itself by a longer route.

TO BE FAIR TO THE LETTER OF THE CRITERION: the test does assert against values passed to the child, it does not compare the record to a recomputation of the record, and it does run under `node scripts/launcher_test.js`, which .github/workflows/scan.yml:45 genuinely executes. Every clause reads as satisfied. The requirement's substance — protection — is what is absent, and protection is what Req 4 asks for. This is the same shape as the note I left on sprint 30 and it is why I left it: the fix chosen made the test cross a real subprocess boundary, which is a genuine strengthening in a different dimension (it caught the missing-instruction mutation below, in-process tests and all), but it does not address the dimension the requirement is about.

THE FIX, AND I CLEARED THE OBSTACLE IN FRONT OF IT RATHER THAN HANDING YOU ONE THAT DOESN'T WORK. The two sources have to actually differ before any test can distinguish them. The way to make them differ is a declared test command, which appends a third entry for a needsTestCommand role. My first attempt at that failed, and the reason is worth knowing:

    headlessLaunchArgs(role, prompt, { root })  ->  headlessPermissionArgs(role)   // root NOT passed

`root` is threaded to readDeclaredMcpConfig(root) four lines below and never to headlessPermissionArgs, so withScratchSettings can declare a test command all day and the permission args still read the real ROOT. That is pre-existing, from sprint 12 (4372ad0), not yours — but it is what blocks the test Req 4 needs.

I tried the one-token fix and checked it for fallout before recommending it:

    ...headlessPermissionArgs(role, root)]
    node scripts/launcher_test.js  ->  ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED   (no fallout)

and with it threaded, a scratch root declaring "node scripts/launcher_test.js" produces:

    args    : Bash(node scripts/run-lifecycle.js *) Bash(python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py *) Bash(node scripts/launcher_test.js *)
    profile : Bash(node scripts/run-lifecycle.js *) Bash(python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py *)

They differ. Then I re-applied the second-source drift on top and the comparison finally fails:

    record === args ?  false      <- the drift is now detectable

So: thread `root` (which also fixes a real half-honored option, since production always passes ROOT and behaviour is unchanged there), then add a test that launches a needsTestCommand role against a scratch root with a declared test command and asserts record.allowedTools equals the args value. Three small pieces, all three verified working here.

Note the subprocess test can't be the one to carry this — ROOT is fixed from __dirname in a real child, so a scratch root can't reach it without copying the tree. Keep your subprocess test exactly as it is, it protects something real; add the divergence check in-process alongside it.

================================================================
WHAT IS MET, AND REQ 2 IS THE BEST WORK IN THIS SPRINT
================================================================

REQ 2 — "a reviewer should be able to point at the single source, not at two places that currently agree." I did the experiment the criterion describes rather than reading for it. One edit, inside HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES only, adding 'Bash(qa1-invented-command *)' to master-controller:

    prompt instruction now names it            : true
    record.instructedCommandForms              : [..., "qa1-invented-command"]
    grep for a second literal of that form     : exactly one hit, line 840, the profile itself

One edit, both consumers changed, no second literal anywhere in scripts/. That is the single source, demonstrated. extractGrantedCommandForms reads the already-assembled --allowedTools string rather than the profile that built it, which is why a dynamically-added grant is swept in identically — the right level to parse at.

REQ 1 — verified across the subprocess boundary, all six roles, with my own regex written in the probe rather than importing yours, against the argv a real child process actually received:

  role                forms   instruction first   every form named   task still present
  master-controller     2           yes                 yes                yes
  dev-team-1            2           yes                 yes                yes
  dev-team-2            2           yes                 yes                yes
  qa1                   2           yes                 yes                yes
  pipeman              15           yes                 yes                yes
  liveqa               14           yes                 yes                yes

Instruction block 537-749 chars ahead of a ~1,200-char task. It reaches the role through the launch, never through an agent file — the named risk, avoided.

The wording is right too, and that is not a small thing here: it says matching "has not been demonstrated to tolerate" an absolute-path variant, rather than asserting it doesn't. After sprint 26 that distinction is the house style, and you kept it.

REQ 3 — instructedCommandForms is parsed from the record's own allowedTools value, present as an empty array rather than omitted when there is no grant. An operator holding only stderr can read the grant and the forms side by side.

One honest limit on that field, worth stating for LiveQA: it reports what the grant parses to, not a readback of the prompt. If the prepending ever broke, the record would still list forms and would be confidently wrong about what the role was told. That is not a live defect — your Req 4 subprocess test asserts the real prompt contains each form, and it caught my no-prepend mutation — but "instructed" claims slightly more than the field measures, and the protection lives in a test rather than in the record.

REQ 5 — confirmed properly, not by eye. Serialized HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES from each commit's own module: 170e7258f788763a… at 82cb7fe and at 17461bb. Byte-identical. No pattern widened, no grant added. Also checked every Bash entry across all six profiles ends with a space-wildcard, so extractGrantedCommandForms' regex covers all of them — a non-wildcard entry would be silently omitted from the instruction, but none exists today.

TESTS — falsified, three ways, against a full repo copy with a green baseline first:
  instruction not prepended        -> 7 tests FAIL, including the Req 4 subprocess test
  instructedCommandForms hardcoded -> 2 tests FAIL
  parser returns only the first form -> 2 tests FAIL
And the recomputation worry about expectedPromptFor is answered by that first result: the five pre-existing tests it feeds did fail when the instruction stopped being prepended, so the helper is not a tautology, it just computes the expectation by a different route than the code under test.

SUITE: ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED. ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED. TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, "Installed 0.2.4".

================================================================
YOUR SCOPE FLAG — RIGHT AGAIN, PREMISE CHECKED
================================================================

npm view: 0.2.3 is published and `latest` points at it. Versions are immutable, so package.json at 0.2.3 would fail Pipeman's publish, and Reqs 1 and 3 both have LiveQA criteria that require a real published install. Necessary for the sprint's own acceptance criteria. Flagging rather than deciding silently is right; this is the second sprint running where the Requirements list omitted a bump every comparable prior sprint carried, so the thing to fix is the template, not your judgment.

CARRIED, INFORMATIONAL
- `root` is half-threaded in headlessLaunchArgs (see above). Pre-existing since sprint 12, harmless in production, and directly in the way of Req 4's fix.
- Long-carried: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string ownedRepository declaration still falls through silently; who commits a QA1 verdict is still Master Controller's open question from sprint 27.

RECOMMENDATION

Back to dev_build for Req 4 only. Thread `root`, add the divergence test, re-run /sprint-qa1 31. Reqs 1, 2, 3 and 5 are done and I don't need to see them again — hand me back the one thing.

PASS: PASS — round 2. Audited 5ca3809 on main. Sprint file re-read fresh and confirmed byte-identical to round 1 (sha256 52aea67a…), so this audit is scoped to what moved: the root threading and the one new test.

THE BLOCKER IS CLOSED, AND I RAN MY OWN MUTATION RATHER THAN TAKING YOURS. Three of them, against a full repo copy with a verified-green baseline first.

  A. My round-1 mutation verbatim — allowedTools rebuilt from HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES
     round 1: ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED (the gap)
     round 2: FAILS, and the new Req 4 test is the one that catches it

  B. A subtler second source I did not ask for — re-calling headlessPermissionArgs(role)
     without root, which under a scratch root yields the profile-only value
     round 2: FAILS, same test

  C. Revert the root threading, leave the test in place
     round 2: FAILS on the test's OWN setup guard, with the diagnostic naming the cause:
     "a declared test command must make the real args differ from the bare profile -- if this
      fails, `root` is not reaching headlessPermissionArgs() and this test cannot distinguish
      anything"

C is the one I want to single out. The defect I found in round 1 was not that a test was missing — it was that a test could be green while proving nothing, because the condition that gave it discriminating power had quietly stopped holding. You wrote the guard that makes that specific failure loud instead of silent, and B shows the test catches a second source that isn't the one I named. That is fixing the class, not the instance.

NO FALLOUT FROM THE THREADING, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSERTED. I emitted the permission record for all six roles at 17461bb and at 5ca3809, normalised out the machine-specific fields, and hashed the set:

  17461bb  88a10a293e9cdef8…
  5ca3809  88a10a293e9cdef8…

Identical. Production always passes ROOT, so threading it changes nothing there, and now that is a measurement rather than a claim in a comment.

REQ 5 STILL HOLDS AT THIS COMMIT — I re-checked rather than assuming a round-2 fix couldn't have touched it. HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES serialized from each commit's own module:

  82cb7fe (sprint 30's base)  170e7258f788763a…
  17461bb (round 1)           170e7258f788763a…
  5ca3809 (round 2)           170e7258f788763a…

No pattern widened, no grant added, across the whole sprint.

CHANGE SURFACE: one line in run-role.js (the `base` construction) plus one test. Reqs 1, 2 and 3 are untouched, so round 1's verification of them stands — the instruction reaching all six roles' real child argv, the single-source experiment where one edit inside the profiles constant moved both consumers, and instructedCommandForms parsed from the record's own allowedTools.

SUITE: ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED. ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED. TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, "Installed 0.2.4".

CARRIED, INFORMATIONAL
- instructedCommandForms still reports what the grant parses to, not a readback of the prompt. Protected by the subprocess test, which asserts the real prompt carries each form — noted again only so LiveQA reads the field for what it measures.
- The `root` half-threading is now fully fixed, so that carried item is closed.
- Long-carried: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string ownedRepository declaration still falls through silently; who commits a QA1 verdict is still Master Controller's open question from sprint 27.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 31, Pipeman ships and publishes 0.2.4. Commit this verdict first.

For LiveQA: Req 1 wants a real launched role to actually receive the instruction — read the first line of the prompt, not just the record. Req 3's test is whether the grant and the instructed form correspond FROM THE STDERR CAPTURE ALONE, without opening the source; if you find yourself checking run-role.js to answer it, that is the criterion failing, not you.
commit=ee49cdf | ci=green: 1 CI run(s) for ee49cdf0afa76b7ef3acf0dbce3c1048cd2991d4 all completed successfully with real steps executed.

PASS: PASS — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.2.4 with real headless launches. Environment: macOS Darwin arm64, claude 2.1.267. 2026-09-10. ~$0.85 in billed runs.

PROVENANCE
0.2.4 on the registry; dist-tags.latest 0.2.4; gitHead ee49cdf0afa76b7ef3acf0dbce3c1048cd2991d4 == last_shipped_commit; zero `reshipped` events. Content check per sprint 13's rule: all 62 published files byte-identical to `git show ee49cdf:<path>`, MISMATCHED 0, tarball sha1 matches the registry's dist.shasum.

================================================================
REQ 3 — ANSWERED FROM THE STDERR CAPTURE ALONE: PASS
================================================================
QA1's framing is the criterion's real test: "if you find yourself opening run-role.js to answer it, that's the criterion failing, not you." I did not open it for this, and did not need to.

A single line of captured stderr, in full:
  PERMISSION_RECORD: {"role":"qa1","cliVersion":"2.1.267","workingDirectory":"/private/tmp/fc31",
  "permissionMode":"acceptEdits","allowedTools":"Bash(node scripts/run-lifecycle.js *) Bash(python3
  scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py *)","disallowedTools":"Edit,Write","mcpConfigSupplied":false,
  "instructedCommandForms":["node scripts/run-lifecycle.js","python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py"]}

The new `instructedCommandForms` field sits beside `allowedTools` in the same record, so the correspondence is checkable in place. Derived mechanically from the capture, stripping `Bash(` and ` *)` from each grant:
  granted    -> Bash(node scripts/run-lifecycle.js *)   Bash(python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py *)
  derived    -> node scripts/run-lifecycle.js           python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py
  instructed -> node scripts/run-lifecycle.js           python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py
  derived == instructed, exactly: True
  every instructed form is covered by a grant: True

An operator holding only this line can confirm that what the role was told to type is what the role was permitted to run. That is the property, and it is visible without source access, which is what the criterion actually asks.

Worth naming why putting both in one record matters more than it looks. Sprint 30 made a denial attributable to a grant. This makes a denial attributable to a *mismatch between the grant and the instruction* — the case where the profile is correct, the role is obedient, and it still gets denied because it was told a form the grant does not cover. That failure is invisible from either field alone and obvious from the two together.

================================================================
REQ 1 (LiveQA half) — A REAL LAUNCHED ROLE RECEIVES IT: PASS, TWO WAYS
================================================================
QA1 asked specifically for the first line of the prompt itself, not just the record. So I captured the child's actual argv with a stub whose only job was to write out what it received, and read the prompt from it.

The child's argv is 15 elements; the composed prompt is the last, 1717 characters. Its FIRST LINE:
  "PERMISSION GRANT -- EXACT COMMAND FORMS REQUIRED: your Bash permission grant for this session
   matches these forms exactly, character for character..."
followed immediately by the two forms, then the role's actual task. The instruction arrives through the launch itself, as argv, and it is the first thing in the prompt rather than buried after the task — a role that reads only the opening still gets it.

THEN THE STRONGER TEST, because receiving text is not the same as acting on it. I launched the same role for real, against a real sprint:
  exit 0, 17 turns, 1 permission denial
  the sprint's own state afterwards: "QA1 audit result: FAIL (rounds: 1)",
  "Last touched by: qa1, session 59425fb3-..."

Recording that verdict requires successfully invoking `node scripts/run-lifecycle.js qa1 ...` — one of the two instructed forms. The state file changed and is attributed to the role's own session, so the form was not merely delivered, it was used, and it worked.

And its single denial was:
  diff <(tail -n +8 .../templates/sprint-template.md) <(tail -n +8 .../sprint-1_invocation-probe.md)
a process-substitution compound, which starts with neither instructed form. So in the same run: instructed forms succeeded, a non-instructed form was refused. That is the instruction and the grant agreeing in practice, observed from behaviour rather than from text.

ONE THING I AM NOT CLAIMING. I noticed this run produced 1 denial in 17 turns where earlier gates of mine produced 2 in 3 and 2 in 17, and it is tempting to read that as the instruction reducing denials. I am not recording it as evidence: different tasks, different repositories, different sprint contents, no control. It is an impression, not a measurement, and this project has spent several sprints establishing why that distinction matters.

================================================================
WHAT I OBSERVED VS ACCEPTED
================================================================
Every result here I produced directly against published 0.2.4. The prompt's first line came from the child's own received argv, captured by a stub, rather than from reading the launcher's composition code. The Req 3 correspondence was derived from the stderr capture only — I have not opened run-role.js in this gate, which was the point. The real-role half was confirmed against the sprint's state file and its session attribution, not against the role's own prose summary of what it did.

Pipeman's note that an unrelated local `.vscode/settings.json` edit sat uncommitted in their tree throughout is acknowledged: it is not in the published tarball (my content check covers all 62 shipped files against the commit) and it is not a sprint artifact, so it has no bearing on this verdict.

No corrections to my own method this round.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================
Ship-ready. The instruction reaches the role through the launch as the first line of its prompt, the role demonstrably uses the forms it was given, and the grant and the instruction now appear together in one stderr line so their correspondence can be checked by someone holding nothing else. Req 3's own test — that the correspondence is visible without source access — is met in the strict sense QA1 framed it.

Nothing carries forward from this sprint. Three items remain open from earlier gates, unchanged: the hollow-green CI case is still unobserved, no role is designated to commit its own verdict, and the permission anchor is now six CLI versions behind this machine.

This PASS means the code is ready, not that anyone is authorized to close sprint 31.
